claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by the ability to trigger controlled transient nanoparticle coalescence.
Transient coalescence activates surface diffusion without requiring full melting.
Coalescence-activated surface diffusion produces a homogenized, single-phase alloy.
Controlled transient coalescence preserves a high fraction of surface atoms.
An intermediate processing condition that causes modest coalescence-induced intermixing minimizes phase separation.
Modest coalescence prevents excessive surface segregation of lower-surface-energy elements.
Au and Cu are examples of lower-surface-energy species in the proposed multimetal systems.
The non-noble constituents of the proposed precursor have higher cohesive energies than its noble-metal constituents.
Preformed small clusters or droplets constitute a state amenable to rapid atomic diffusion.
Differences in surface energy drive diffusion in the nanoparticle surface and near-surface regions.
During transient coalescence, enhanced but kinetically limited diffusion is driven by surface-energy minimization.
Excessive heating leads to elemental segregation or phase separation.
A process that is too rapid leads to significant segregation or phase separation.
Au and Cu migrate preferentially to the nanoparticle surface during thermal structural evolution.
A brief, moderate coalescence step will yield nanoparticles with minimal elemental segregation.
A baseline process that bypasses controlled transient coalescence will produce pronounced phase separation.
The baseline process will enrich Au and Cu at the nanoparticle surface.
Surface enrichment and segregation compromise uniform catalytic activity.
The proposed mechanism applies particularly to systems containing more than five noble and non-noble elements with disparate surface energies.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to binary or ternary systems or to systems in which thermal-stability constraints preclude coalescence.
